opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a real difference, though perhaps not as large as people sometimes assume.

With the classic object-recognition networks, the ones trained on ImageNet, the task is very narrow. You give the system an image and it produces a label: "this is a cheetah," "this is a school bus." For a long time people said these systems "understand" images, but when you look closely, a lot of what they're doing is picking up on texture and local statistical regularities rather than anything like the structure of the scene. That's why you get adversarial examples, where you change a few pixels imperceptibly and suddenly the school bus is classified as an ostrich with 99% confidence. A system that understood what a school bus is, that it has wheels and windows and a certain shape and function, wouldn't make that kind of mistake. So I'd say those networks were doing very sophisticated pattern classification, not understanding.

The text-and-image models are interesting because they connect visual input to language, and language carries a great deal of structure: objects, relations, attributes, actions. So in principle a system that can map between an image and a rich description has to represent more of what's going on. You can ask it, "What is the man to the left of the dog holding?" That's a much richer interface than a single label.

But when you probe these systems, you still find that the understanding is often shallow. Ask an image generator for "a red cube on top of a blue sphere" and you may well get a blue cube on a red sphere, or the two objects side by side. Compositional structure, meaning who is doing what to whom, what is on top of what, how many of something there are, is exactly where they tend to break down. That suggests they're still largely associating bags of concepts with bags of visual features, rather than building something like a model of the scene with objects and relations.

So I'd describe it as moving from a very impoverished interface to a much richer one, and that's genuine progress. But I don't think we've crossed the line into what I'd call real scene understanding: knowing that there are persistent objects in a three-dimensional world, with properties and relationships, that obey physical constraints. I think that still requires representations with more explicit structure than these systems have, and I suspect that's one reason they need such enormous amounts of data to get the performance they do. A child learns what a giraffe is from one or two picture-book examples. That kind of data efficiency comes from having the right structured representations to begin with.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that in both cases we should be careful about the word "understanding." An object-recognition network, say the classic ImageNet-style classifier, is doing something quite narrow. It learns a mapping from pixels to a label, and it does that remarkably well on the distribution it was trained on. But it has no notion that the cat in the picture is a three-dimensional object that persists over time, that it could walk behind the sofa, that it has a front and a back. If you rotate the object, change the lighting, put it in an unusual context, performance can fall apart in ways that would never happen to a human child. And we know from adversarial examples that what the network is keying on is often not what we would call the object at all. It's picking up on texture, on statistical regularities that happen to correlate with the label.

The text-and-image models are more interesting, because the language side forces a kind of compositional structure onto the representation. If you can describe a scene as "a man in a red hat standing to the left of a bicycle," the model has to have some internal representation where "red" attaches to the hat and not the bicycle, where "left of" is a relation between two things. So you get something that looks more like the beginnings of a scene description rather than just a label. And you can query it. You can ask what's happening, or what would happen next, and sometimes you get sensible answers.

But I would still resist saying these systems understand images in the sense that we do. What's missing, in my view, is an underlying model of the world: objects, physics, causality, the fact that things have insides and weights and purposes. When a human looks at a picture of a kitchen, they're not retrieving captions. They're reconstructing a situation in which they could act, in which they know the stove is hot and the drawer opens and the glass will break if it falls. The vision-language models have absorbed an enormous amount of text about kitchens, so they can often produce the right words. But the gap between producing the right words and actually having the model that generates those words is exactly the gap we don't know how to measure well yet. And I think a lot of the confusion in the field comes from treating fluent output as evidence of the underlying competence, when it may just be evidence of having seen a great deal of similar output.

So the difference is real, and it's progress. The multimodal systems are grounded in a way the pure classifiers never were. But I'd put it as going from a lookup table to a very sophisticated statistical description, rather than going from no understanding to understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says classifiers can rely on texture and statistical regularities correlated with labels rather than the object itself, and that performance can fail in unusual contexts.

r002.rationale: The response describes compositional scene descriptions and relations, but does not say text-and-image models recombine image components into new images or use that as evidence of parsing.

astra-6.text:
Well, object recognition is a fairly narrow task. You show the system an image, and it says, “That’s a dog.” And it can be extremely good at that without being able to say much about what the dog is doing, why it’s doing it, or what might happen next.

With text-and-image models, you can ask much more open-ended questions. What’s happening in this scene? What’s unusual about it? How do the different objects relate to one another? So there’s a much richer connection between the visual input and the kinds of concepts we express in language.

But we have to be careful about calling that understanding. If a system gives a plausible description, is it actually extracting those relationships from the image, or is it supplying what usually goes with that sort of scene? Those can look very similar until you ask a question where the particular details matter. So I think the capabilities are much broader, but the extent to which they reflect a coherent understanding of the physical world remains an open question.

r002.rationale: The response discusses open-ended questions about scenes and relationships, but does not mention recombining image components into new images as evidence of parsing them.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, an object-recognition network is typically trained to take an image and assign a label to it: “That’s a dog,” or “That’s a bicycle.” And it can be extremely good at that without necessarily understanding much about what’s happening in the image.

With a text-and-image model, you can ask much more varied questions. What is this person doing? How are these objects related? What’s unusual about this scene? So there’s a much richer connection between the visual input and the concepts we express in language.

But we have to be careful about what we infer from that. Producing a plausible description doesn’t necessarily mean that the system has a coherent understanding of the scene. You might get a very impressive answer to one question, and then discover, with a follow-up question, that it hasn’t understood some fairly basic spatial or causal relationship. So I think it’s a significant broadening of capability, but whether that amounts to understanding is something you have to investigate, rather than assume from the fluency of the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says object-recognition networks assign image labels but does not say they can rely on contextual cues instead of features of the object.
